transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Yeah, thanks. I guess the big reason is… I keep running into this wall with work that takes real sit-down thinking. Like monthly reports, planning bigger things, especially when it’s across multiple sites—health events and that kind of thing.

I know it matters, and I’m not trying to blow it off, but I’ll just keep putting it off. I’ll find other things to do, answer emails, check on some operational thing, talk to someone about a totally different issue—actually last week I spent way too long dealing with a vendor thing that probably could’ve waited—but the report I needed to finish just sat there.

So, yeah, that’s mainly why I’m here. It’s getting frustrating.
Have you noticed this kind of difficulty focusing and putting off tasks going back to when you were a kid or in school, or is this something that's really only become a problem more recently?

Yeah, it definitely goes back. I mean, I didn’t think of it that way at the time—I was just a kid—but in elementary school my teachers would tell my parents I was bright, but I was always kind of… off in my own head.

I’d lose worksheets all the time, and homework would just not make it back to school unless my mom basically checked my backpack every night. She had this whole routine with me at the kitchen table, and I remember hating it because I wanted to go do literally anything else. So yeah, it’s not totally new. It’s just showing up bigger now with work stuff.
Do you often feel restless, fidgety, or have trouble sitting still, or find yourself acting or speaking impulsively without thinking it through?

I don’t know that I’m like… physically restless all the time. But the talking part, yeah, that happens.

Usually it’s when I’m nervous because I dropped the ball on something. Like if I make a scheduling mistake, I’ll start explaining what happened, and then I keep explaining it—like way past the point where the other person clearly already understands. I can see it on their face sometimes, like, “Okay, got it,” and I’m still going because I’m trying to make sure they know I didn’t mean to mess it up.

And then afterward I’m like, why did I keep talking? I probably made it worse.

Aside from talking too much when nervous, do you often find yourself fidgeting, tapping your hands or feet, or feeling like you need to get up and move around even in situations where you're expected to stay seated, like meetings?

Um… I don’t really know. I’m not sure I’ve noticed that as a big thing.

Like, in meetings I might shift around or mess with a pen, but I feel like everybody does that, especially when the meeting is going long or someone’s going through a spreadsheet line by line. We have these meetings where it’s supposed to be 30 minutes and then suddenly it’s an hour, and half the time we’re talking about something that probably could’ve been an email—sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

I guess I don’t usually feel like I have to get up and move. Not in a strong way. It’s more… I might be uncomfortable or bored, but I can stay seated.
Outside of work, do you also notice yourself losing track of things, forgetting appointments, or struggling to stay organized in your personal life—like at home or in your daily routines?

Yeah, it’s not just work. It shows up with personal stuff too.

Like, I help out with some community events, and I’ll forget to return calls from volunteers, or there’ll be some small errand I said I’d do—pick something up, follow up with somebody—and then it just… disappears from my head. And then later something reminds me and I get that sinking feeling.

There have been once or twice where a community meeting completely slipped my mind until someone texted me, like, “Are you coming?” And then I’m scrambling and apologizing. I hate that, because I don’t want people thinking I don’t care or I’m blowing them off.
Have you been experiencing any persistent feelings of sadness, anxiety, or excessive worry recently that might be affecting your concentration?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I get worried when I’ve forgotten something or I’m behind, but I don’t know if that’s like… anxiety-anxiety, or just reacting to the mess I made, you know?

I wouldn’t say I’ve been walking around sad all the time. It’s more like I get frustrated with myself. And then I’ll spend too long thinking about why I forgot the thing, or whether someone’s annoyed with me—especially with work stuff, because in healthcare management there are so many moving parts, and if one person doesn’t get called back then suddenly three other people are waiting on it.

Sorry, I’m kind of drifting. I guess the short answer is I haven’t noticed some big constant sadness or worry driving the concentration problems. It feels more like the concentration thing comes first, and then I worry afterward.

Would you say these forgetfulness and follow-through issues have actually caused real problems—like conflicts, missed opportunities, or people being upset with you—both at work and in your personal life?

Yeah… I mean, I’m not getting fired or anything, and I still show up and do the things I’m supposed to do—mostly. But yes, it has caused problems.

At work, there have been times where a deadline slipped because I didn’t follow up when I said I would, or someone else had to step in and remind a department or make the call I forgot to make. And that’s embarrassing, because in my role you’re supposed to be the person keeping the pieces moving, not the person other people are chasing.

And outside of work too. With community stuff or friends, I’ve had to send those last-minute “I’m so sorry, I completely forgot” messages, which just feels awful. People have been nice about it, mostly, but I can tell sometimes they’re frustrated, or they’ve had to cover for the gap I left. So… yeah, I’m getting by, but it’s not like there are no consequences.
Do you often find yourself interrupting conversations, finishing other people's sentences, or making decisions quickly without really thinking them through?

I’m not sure that’s really my thing. I mean, I might jump in sometimes if I think I know where someone’s going, but I don’t think people would describe me as constantly interrupting or making snap decisions.

Actually, I tend to go the other way sometimes—like I’ll sit on a decision too long because I’m trying to remember all the pieces, and then… well, now I’m getting off track. But no, the interrupting or blurting stuff hasn’t stood out to me the way the forgetting and follow-through problems have.

Do you often find that even when someone is talking directly to you—like in a one-on-one conversation or meeting—your mind starts to wander and you lose track of what they're saying, or people notice you seem distracted or 'somewhere else'?

Yeah, that does happen. It’s kind of embarrassing because I’ll be looking right at the person, like I’m listening, and then my brain just… grabs onto something else.

In meetings, for example, someone will be giving a budget update, and I really do mean to follow it, but then a phone vibrates, or there are people talking out in the hallway, or I suddenly remember something I forgot to do for the league, and I’m gone. Not physically, obviously, but I’ll miss the next few minutes and then come back in not totally sure what they just said.

And then I’m trying to piece it together from context, which sometimes works, but sometimes I have to ask them to repeat it. Or I just nod along for a second, which I know isn’t great.

Thinking back to childhood specifically before age 12, do you remember these attention and forgetfulness problems actually causing you trouble—like losing things, not finishing schoolwork, or getting in trouble for it—rather than just being a personality trait people noticed?

Yeah, I think it did cause trouble even then. I remember in elementary school, the way teachers would put it to my parents was always like, “He’s bright, but…” and then the “but” was that I was daydreaming all the time, or I’d lose worksheets, or I wouldn’t turn homework in.

And it wasn’t like I didn’t do any of it. Sometimes it was literally in my backpack, just crumpled up in a folder or stuck between papers, and my mom would have to check my backpack every night to make sure things actually got turned in. Which—funny, I can still picture that backpack, it had this awful zipper that always caught on the fabric—but yeah, the point is, if she wasn’t checking, stuff just didn’t make it from home to the teacher. So yes, it was more than just “that’s how he is.” It caused problems at school.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure that’s really my thing. I mean, I might jump in sometimes if I think I know where someone’s going, but I don’t think people would describe me as constantly interrupting or making snap decisions.

Actually, I tend to go the other way sometimes—like I’ll sit on a decision too long because I’m trying to remember all the pieces, and then… well, now I’m getting off track. But no, the interrupting or blurting stuff hasn’t stood out to me the way the forgetting and follow-through problems have.

inference.note: Predominantly inattentive symptoms (forgetfulness, poor follow-through, distractibility, disorganization) with childhood onset and cross-situational impairment support ADHD; hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (fidgeting, interrupting, restlessness) are largely absent, but talkativeness when anxious and mild impulsivity in decision-making keep combined presentation from being fully ruled out. Mood/anxiety disorders remain unlikely as primary cause since worry appears secondary to attentional lapses rather than pervasive.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient frequently seems to not listen or loses track when others are speaking directly to him, a core inattentive ADHD symptom not yet explored, to help confirm the diagnostic threshold for inattentive symptoms.
doctor.question: Do you often find that even when someone is talking directly to you—like in a one-on-one conversation or meeting—your mind starts to wander and you lose track of what they're saying, or people notice you seem distracted or 'somewhere else'?

target_item.name: Distractibility
target_item.manifestation: In meetings, I’ll be trying to listen to a budget update, but a phone vibrating, people talking in the hall, or even a thought about something I forgot for the league pulls me away and I miss the next few minutes.
target_item.reason: The question is about losing track during conversations or meetings because the mind wanders or distractions pull attention away, which matches distractibility.

patient.answer:
Yeah, that does happen. It’s kind of embarrassing because I’ll be looking right at the person, like I’m listening, and then my brain just… grabs onto something else.

In meetings, for example, someone will be giving a budget update, and I really do mean to follow it, but then a phone vibrates, or there are people talking out in the hallway, or I suddenly remember something I forgot to do for the league, and I’m gone. Not physically, obviously, but I’ll miss the next few minutes and then come back in not totally sure what they just said.

And then I’m trying to piece it together from context, which sometimes works, but sometimes I have to ask them to repeat it. Or I just nod along for a second, which I know isn’t great.

inference.note: Continued predominantly inattentive symptoms (distractibility, forgetfulness, poor follow-through, losing track in conversations) with childhood onset and functional impairment across settings, while hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (fidgeting, interrupting, restlessness) remain minimal/absent. This supports ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation, consistent with prior candidate; mood/anxiety disorders remain unlikely given the patient's own framing that worry follows rather than causes the concentration issues.

doctor.intent: Confirm DSM-5 age-of-onset criterion by clarifying whether significant inattentive symptoms and their impact were clearly present before age 12, not just vaguely 'always there'
doctor.question: Thinking back to childhood specifically before age 12, do you remember these attention and forgetfulness problems actually causing you trouble—like losing things, not finishing schoolwork, or getting in trouble for it—rather than just being a personality trait people noticed?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even in elementary school, my teachers told my parents I was bright but always daydreaming, losing worksheets, and forgetting to turn in homework unless my mother checked my backpack every night.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically whether the attention and forgetfulness problems were present and impairing before age 12.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I think it did cause trouble even then. I remember in elementary school, the way teachers would put it to my parents was always like, “He’s bright, but…” and then the “but” was that I was daydreaming all the time, or I’d lose worksheets, or I wouldn’t turn homework in.

And it wasn’t like I didn’t do any of it. Sometimes it was literally in my backpack, just crumpled up in a folder or stuck between papers, and my mom would have to check my backpack every night to make sure things actually got turned in. Which—funny, I can still picture that backpack, it had this awful zipper that always caught on the fabric—but yeah, the point is, if she wasn’t checking, stuff just didn’t make it from home to the teacher. So yes, it was more than just “that’s how he is.” It caused problems at school.

inference.note: Childhood onset confirmed with functional impairment before age 12 (lost worksheets, incomplete homework, needed parental oversight), plus persistent inattentive symptoms (distractibility, forgetfulness, poor follow-through, mind-wandering) causing impairment across work and personal domains in adulthood. Hyperactive-impulsive symptoms remain minimal (no significant fidgeting, no interrupting/blurting, no rash decision-making), consistent with predominantly inattentive presentation of ADHD. Mood/anxiety disorders ruled out as primary explanation since patient denies persistent sadness or excessive worry independent of the attention difficulties.

opening_question.intent: Establish the primary reason for the visit today
opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a lifelong pattern (childhood onset, before age 12) of significant inattentive symptoms—losing items, poor task follow-through, forgetfulness, distractibility, avoidance of sustained mental effort—that persist into adulthood and cause functional impairment across work and personal/community domains. Hyperactive-impulsive symptoms are minimal (no significant motor restlessness, no impulsive decision-making/interrupting), though some excessive talking when anxious is noted, insufficient to meet combined presentation criteria. Anxiety/mood symptoms are secondary and reactive to the attentional difficulties rather than primary, making a mood/anxiety disorder less likely as the primary diagnosis. This pattern is consistent with ADHD, Predominantly Inattentive Presentation (F90.0).
